analysis:
Examined ProviderConfig.swift and CoordinatorClient+Registration.swift.

ProviderConfig.swift (head lines 161-167, 343-344, 372, 383, 427, 482): adds an optional `autopilotDownloads: AutopilotDownloadSettings?` field under `[backend.autopilot_downloads]`, with CodingKey, decodeIfPresent, encodeIfPresent and an init parameter defaulting to nil. It is operator-local configuration and does not touch coordinator trust, attestation, keys or cache crypto. The comment says it is not consent and never bumps the Autopilot revision. The settings type is not in the supplied evidence, so I could not check what its semantics allow. Possible concerns for the next pass: whether download caps or reserve values are validated; whether a malicious local operator (ADV-001) or a coordinator-driven download request can bypass them (disk fill, T-016); and whether defaults of 'on, no caps' enlarge the download attack surface (model weights, A-004, T-012). These are unverified, so I am not filing a finding.

CoordinatorClient+Registration.swift (head lines ~26-45, 69-71): refactors registration to build a typed message via `registrationMessage` and encode it through `ProviderProtocolCodec.encodeProviderMessage`. Registration now reads `state.modelAutopilotRegistration`, which returns a snapshot and inventory together. That is a single atomic read, and it removes a possible skew between the two reads. After the send it records `state.registeredAutopilotInventoryIDs` from the message actually sent. The write happens only after the blocking send completes without throwing, so it reflects what was transmitted. The appAttestResumeNonce handling is unchanged: it is still attached only when `nwConnection === connection`. The registration frame contents and the TB-002 wire contract look unchanged, apart from the new autopilot inventory handling, which already existed. The `registeredAutopilotInventoryIDs` consumer is not in the supplied evidence. The question to check is whether it is used to authorize or validate later coordinator-requested download or preload operations. If so, state staleness across reconnects would matter (compare T-053). I found no concrete regression.

The supplied evidence does not show the codec, the state type or the settings type, so integration should confirm them.
